title: Creatify Space
summary: A portfolio builder that turns a LinkedIn PDF into a personal website you can edit and share with one link.

story.title: The Project
text: Creatify Space helps people without design or coding skills get a portfolio online. You upload your LinkedIn PDF and the app turns it into a personal website with its own shareable link.
I built it on my own for a school assignment, from idea to working product.

story.title: My Role
text: I did everything myself: the design in Figma and the full application in Next.js. That includes the PDF import, the editing dashboard, authentication, the database and the portfolio generation.

story.title: Behind the Work
text: The hard part was turning a LinkedIn PDF into something users can actually edit. Pulling the text out was only the first step. I also had to sort it into the right portfolio sections and keep every part editable.
For login I used passwordless magic links, and Prisma with PostgreSQL stores the user data. I wanted it to feel simple for the user, even with a lot happening behind the scenes.

story.title: The Outcome
text: A working portfolio generator where users import their info, personalize their profile and publish a portfolio they can share.
It gave me experience building a whole application on my own, and I learned the most about authentication, PDF parsing and working with a database.

title: Tasbeeh Challenge
summary: A mobile-first app that makes daily dhikr more engaging with challenges, streaks and friendly competition.

story.title: The Project
text: Tasbeeh Challenge started with my sister. She wanted to compete with her friends over who could do the most dhikr (repeating short prayers), and I thought it would be fun to build an app for that.
You can count your dhikr, complete challenges, track your progress and compete with friends on a leaderboard. I built it in my free time, just because I liked the idea.

story.title: My Role
text: I designed and built the whole app myself, from the interface and user flows to the functionality behind it.
That includes the challenge system, the interactive counter, progress tracking, leaderboards and profiles, plus Google sign-in and Firebase for storing user data.

story.title: Behind the Work
text: People would use it on their phones every day, so I made it mobile-first, kept the counter quick and satisfying, and added PWA support so it can be installed like an app. Challenges, streaks and points give users something to work towards.
The trickiest part was connecting everything through Firebase. Finishing a challenge has to update the user's progress, points and the leaderboard without making the app feel complicated.

story.title: The Outcome
text: A working app with dhikr counters, challenges, progress statistics, profiles and friend and community leaderboards.

I got more practice building a complete application independently, especially Firebase authentication and storing user progress. What I like most is that it came from a simple conversation. I didn't need an assignment to start building something useful.

title: MoodTunes
summary: An app that reads your mood through your camera and builds a Spotify playlist that matches it, or helps you change it.

story.title: The Project
text: MoodTunes detects how you feel through your camera and creates a Spotify playlist for it. The twist: you choose whether you want music that matches your mood or music that helps you change it.
The idea was mine. I pitched it to my classmates and we built it together as a school project.

story.title: My Role
text: I came up with the concept and designed the UI together with a classmate. I handled the frontend styling (playful colors, typography and interactions) and built the Spotify authentication, the API integration and the choice step.
A teammate built the facial emotion detection.

story.title: Behind the Work
text: Your current mood isn't always how you want to feel. Someone who feels sad might want uplifting music, so we added a choice step before the playlist is generated.
My main challenge was the Spotify integration and connecting the user's choices to the playlist, while keeping the different screens consistent and easy to follow.

story.title: The Outcome
text: A working prototype that combines facial emotion detection, user preferences and Spotify playlist generation.

I gained experience with external APIs and interactive frontend features. Seeing my own idea turn into a working app was the best part, and it showed me what a team can do when everyone brings different skills.

title: VECOZO
summary: A healthcare app that brings consultation planning and patient information together in one place, built for VECOZO.

story.title: The Project
text: VECOZO is a Dutch organization that helps healthcare professionals share information securely. For a school assignment, our team of six built an application for multidisciplinary consultations (MDOs), where specialists from different fields discuss patient cases.
We had 12 weeks to deliver a working prototype that makes it easier to plan consultations and manage patient information in one place.

story.title: My Role
text: I worked on both design and development. I designed the whole interface in Figma, including layouts, visual style and reusable components, and built core features in C# connected to the application's logic and data.
I also helped teammates build and refine other parts of the application.

story.title: Behind the Work
text: Healthcare professionals need to work efficiently, so I focused on clear navigation, patient information that is easy to find and fewer steps for common tasks.

The app is built with C# and MSSQL in a layered architecture that separates presentation, business logic and data access. We worked in sprints with two project days a week and presented to VECOZO every four weeks. Their feedback decided what we improved next.

story.title: The Outcome
text: A working prototype that brings patient management, consultation planning and MDO discussions into one application.

I became more confident with C#, learned how to structure an application in layers and got to work with a real client. My biggest takeaway: balance design and development, and keep the people who use the software at the center.

title: Restaurant GEM
summary: A custom WordPress website designed in Figma to capture the restaurant's atmosphere, built so the client can manage the content themselves.

story.title: The Project
text: Restaurant GEM is a restaurant website I worked on during my internship at Unique Design. It had to capture the restaurant's atmosphere, from the imagery and typography to how visitors move through the site, while making practical information like the menu and reservations easy to find.

story.title: My Role
text: I designed everything in Figma and built most of it as a custom WordPress theme with PHP, Bootstrap and Advanced Custom Fields (ACF), so the client can update their content on their own.
A coworker helped with the page transitions and animations. I did the rest, from layouts and responsive styling to the WordPress implementation.

story.title: Behind the Work
text: I wanted it to feel like more than a restaurant template, so I put a lot of attention into typography, photography and spacing, while keeping the menu and reservation information easy to reach.
Because it is a custom theme, I made sure it works across screen sizes and stays flexible when the client changes content through ACF.

story.title: The Outcome
text: A custom WordPress website that turns my Figma designs into a working site the client can manage. It was also nominated for Site of the Day on Awwwards.

I learned how to take a client project from design through development, build flexible PHP templates and work with a coworker on the finishing details. It let me bring my design and development skills together.

title: Pomotomo
summary: A focus timer that grows a virtual plant as you study, with a physical buzzer that goes off when your session ends.

story.title: The Project
text: Pomotomo is a focus app we built as a team for a school project. It uses the Pomodoro technique: you study for a set time and then take a short break.
To make focusing more rewarding, a virtual plant grows with every finished session. A physical buzzer tells you when time is up, so you don't have to keep checking the screen.

story.title: My Role
text: I designed the interface in Figma together with a teammate, then worked on the app with the team. We built the website with ASP.NET and C#, and SQLite stores the user accounts and completed focus sessions.
It includes the focus timer, a virtual garden and a statistics page that shows how much time you have spent studying.

story.title: Behind the Work
text: The interesting part was connecting the website to a real piece of hardware. The timer has to tell the buzzer when a session is over.
We also linked completed sessions to the plant's growth and the user's statistics, so every part of the app works together.

story.title: The Outcome
text: A working Pomodoro app with focus and break timers, a growing virtual plant, a physical buzzer and progress tracking.
This project was different from my others because something physical was connected to the website. It wasn't only about what happened on the screen.
